piece.caption: Why basic AI automation won't give your Indian business a competitive advantage. Building a basic AI prototype or simple workflow automation is easier than ever. However, if a tool can be copied in days by anyone, it will not create long-term business value. Investors and tech experts emphasize that lasting value comes from domain expertise, proprietary distribution networks, and embedding AI deep into your operational systems of record. Before spending money on standalone AI tools, evaluate if they integrate with your core workflows and protect sensitive customer data. Comment CHECKLIST for our 4-step AI evaluation framework.

claims.claim: AI has reduced the manpower needed to build a minimum viable product or demo, making software development more accessible.
Products that can be easily replicated within days struggle to retain customers and fail to create lasting value.
Long-term value in enterprise AI comes from deep integration into business operations and specialized domain expertise.
Data governance and security must be prioritized early when handling sensitive enterprise or customer data.

piece.dm_text: Here is the 4-step framework to evaluate AI tools before buying: 1. Uniqueness check: Can a competitor replicate this tool setup in a few days? 2. Operational depth: Does the tool embed directly into your system of record, or is it a standalone workflow? 3. Domain edge: Does it leverage specific industry expertise that gives you a moat? 4. Data governance: Are security and data handling configured from day one for sensitive data?

ADVERTISEMENT Seed funding’s new reality check in the age of AI | YourStory AI has made it easier for founders to build products, test ideas, reach customers and, in some cases, generate revenue earlier. But as the barriers to starting a company fall, are investors raising the bar for their first institutional cheque?
This was the central question at ‘First Cheque, Harder Questions: The New Seed Playbook’, a panel discussion at TechSparks 2026.
The session featured Yoonmin Cho, APJ Lead, Snowflake for Startups; Shashank Randev, Founder and General Partner, 247VC; and Anvesh Ramineni, Venture Partner, Endiya. Moderated by Shubhangi Mishra, Senior Creative Lead, YourStory, the discussion examined what investors now expect at the seed stage and whether traditional startup metrics still hold the same weight.
Cho said AI has changed the venture capital ecosystem, particularly after a period of slower funding. At Snowflake, there is considerable interest in enterprise AI, especially vertical AI, along with emerging opportunities in frontier AI.
While AI has made product development more accessible, Cho said founders still need to focus on business fundamentals. A clear competitive advantage, whether through domain expertise, distribution or other strengths, is increasingly important.
Randev said AI is also changing how investors evaluate enterprise technology companies.
Advances in AI are helping deeptech startups develop prototypes and move towards product-market fit faster, but enterprise technology faces a different challenge. AI is replacing several standalone enterprise products, making it harder to identify which solutions will remain relevant over time.
“I think it’s becoming a little more tricky to understand which product in an enterprise tech ecosystem will survive a five-year journey,” he said.
Randev added that AI has disrupted enterprise technology models that have existed for 10–15 years, complicating how investors assess individual products and their place in the value chain.
Ramineni agreed that AI has reduced the manpower needed to build a minimum viable product (MVP) or demo. However, because similar technology is available to everyone, a working product is no longer enough to stand out.
“What founders really need to work on is beyond the product itself. What do they bring to the table that can set them apart from everyone building in the same industry?” he said.
Ramineni also sees an opportunity for Indian startups in vertical AI.
While India may not have foundational AI capabilities comparable to companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic, it has considerable domain expertise.
He cited semiconductor design, noting that 30% of the global semiconductor design workforce is based in India. Access to specialized talent and industry knowledge could help Indian startups build competitive vertical AI applications.
With MVPs becoming easier to develop, investors are looking more closely at the founders, the problems they are solving, and their competitive advantages.
For Cho, the starting point is understanding customers and identifying problems they are willing to pay to solve.
She said startups must approach their work as businesses rather than simply product-development exercises. Founders need to understand customer pain points and workflows, build strong teams, and develop expertise that competitors cannot easily replicate.
They must also provide tangible evidence of why their businesses can succeed.
Randev outlined five parameters he considers when evaluating startups: the founders’ backgrounds and complementary skills; their understanding of the total addressable market (TAM) and go-to-market strategy; the business model; intellectual property or other competitive advantages; and the value investors can add after investing.
In deeptech, he said, teams need both technical expertise and the ability to build a business.
However, founder vision remains particularly important.
“At least one founder needs to have a vision. Without that, it’s very difficult for VCs to inculcate that vision. We are backing the founder,” Randev said.
He referred to investments in the battery ecosystem, plastic segregation robotics, and 3D metal printing. Despite operating in specialized sectors, the founders shared a clear vision of what they wanted to build and how they intended to grow their companies.
Ramineni said MVPs and demos have become basic expectations rather than reasons to invest.
Founders must demonstrate an advantage that competitors cannot easily copy. This could come from proprietary distribution networks, deep domain expertise, or an established reputation in their industry.
A product that another company can replicate within days is unlikely to provide a lasting advantage, although deeptech and biotech businesses differ because of their underlying technology.
In enterprise AI, Ramineni said investors are also looking beyond basic workflow automation.
Products that can be easily replicated or replaced may struggle to retain customers. Instead, solutions that become embedded in an enterprise's operations are more likely to create long-term value.
He pointed to systems of record that build a context layer around an organization’s business processes. As these systems become more closely integrated with operations, they become harder to replace.
Data governance: A priority from day one?
As startups adopt AI, data governance, security, and infrastructure are becoming important considerations. But should founders prioritize these before achieving product-market fit?
Cho said the answer depends on the product and its customers.
“If you’re building a product that deals with sensitive data, or you’re working with enterprise customers, you definitely need to think about the governance and safety, security from the beginning,” she said.
Addressing these requirements later can be considerably more expensive, particularly for companies handling sensitive information or serving enterprise customers.
Cho cited a company that invested in a stable data platform after its CTO recognized the time and resources involved in repeatedly hiring, training, and replacing engineers to manage its data infrastructure.
The decision was based on the company’s business priorities rather than the technology itself.
She said founders should make infrastructure and platform decisions based on business needs, particularly when those investments help them operate more efficiently, move faster, and reach customers sooner.
The discussion also examined the indicators investors now consider when evaluating seed-stage startups.
For Cho, repeat users are an important sign of sustained customer demand.
Randev looks for customer retention and recurring engagement in enterprise and consumer technology businesses. However, he said deeptech and advanced manufacturing startups can still attract investment at the prototype stage.
